1:
The title is challenged before the psalm is read. Clarke reports the objection: that the psalm "was not written on the occasion to which the title refers, is evident from" verse 4, which "ill suits the case of David, who laid a successful plot against Uriah's life, after he had defiled his bed", and from verse 18, which prays for walls David never saw broken. Delitzsch defends the ascription and turns its awkwardness into evidence: "the carelessness of the Hebrew style shows itself in the fact that one and the same phrase is used of Nathan's coming in an official capacity to David and of David's going in unto Bathsheba". He places it as "the first of the Davidic Elohim-Psalms".

Henry and Calvin take the occasion as given and make it the psalm's whole force. Henry calls the sin "the inlet to all the other sins that followed; it was as the letting forth of water", recorded "for warning to all, that he who thinks he stands may take heed lest he fall"; and he marks the interval, David going "above nine months... without any particular expressions of remorse". Calvin describes the same lethargy — David "would seem to have sunk into a spiritual lethargy" until "roused from it by the expostulation of Nathan" — and gives the psalm a public purpose: to "testify his repentance to all around him, and leave some lasting proof of it to posterity".

Spurgeon fixes on the order of the opening words: "he appeals at once to the mercy of God, even before he mentions his sin. The sight of mercy is good for eyes sore with penitential weeping." Pardon "must ever be an act of pure mercy, and therefore to that attribute the awakened sinner flies"; the plea is that God "act, O Lord, like thyself." He reads the multitude of tender mercies as asking God to "reveal all thy gentlest attributes in my case, not only in their essence but in their abundance." Gill makes the same point about direction: David "under a sense of sin, does not run away from God, but applies unto him, and casts himself at his feet".

Ellicott works the vocabulary. Blot out is "most probably... taken from the custom of erasing a written record"; but the prophet uses it differently — "I will blot out thy sins as a cloud" — which yields "a fine thought that the error and guilt that cloud the mind and conscience can be cleared off like a mist by a breath from heaven". Transgression implies "a wilful throwing off of authority or restraint", perhaps "the breach of the covenant-relation irrespective of any particular sin", so the prayer is that God act "according to His chesed or covenant-favour, and wipe out from His records whatever has intervened between the covenant parties."

On "wash me throughly" the three who touch it agree on the intensive, differ on the image. Clarke renders it "wash me again and again... My stain is deep; ordinary purgation will not be sufficient." Gill reads long habitation: the sin "had long lain upon him... and therefore he needed much washing". Ellicott alone separates the two verbs, which "are not merely antithetic": wash means literally to tread, "describing the process of washing clothes (as blankets are washed to this day in Scotland) by trampling them with the feet", while cleanse is the priest's "formal declaration of cleanliness" in leprosy.

Delitzsch supplies the theology the petition rests on: "true penitence is not a dead knowledge of sin committed, but a living sensitive consciousness of it, to which it is ever present as a matter and ground of unrest and pain." He then guards it against misuse: this sorrow "is, it is true, no merit that wins mercy or favour, but it is the condition, without which it is impossible for any manifestation of favour to take place."
3:
Confession is a state, not an act. Clarke marks it diagnostic: "a true, deep, and unsophisticated mark of a genuine penitent. Wherever he turns his face, he sees his sin, and through it the eye of an angry God." Ellicott keeps his distinction between the two nouns — the general breach of covenant, then "the offence which made the breach" — reading an accusing conscience that keeps the sin "always before his eyes".

"Against thee, thee only" is the psalm's hardest clause, and produces three incompatible solutions. Wesley makes it comparative: the words are "not to be understood absolutely, because he had sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah, and many others; but comparatively... nothing is more grievous to me, than that I have sinned against thee." Clarke grants the objection its force — the matter of Bathsheba and Uriah "could not be said to have been committed against God only", being "a public sin... against society at large, as well as against the peace, honor, comfort, and life of an innocent, brave, and patriotic man" — then saves the title by David's office, since as king he "was not liable to be called to account by any of his subjects". Ellicott takes it decisively the other way: the clause "can refer to nothing but a breach of the covenant-relation by the nation at large. An individual would have felt his guilt against the nation or other individuals, as well as against Jehovah." Gill dissolves the problem: all sin, "though committed against a fellow creature, being a transgression of the law, is against the lawgiver".

Wesley reads the justifying clause as a consequence accepted in advance: "whatsoever severities thou shalt use towards me, it will be no blemish to thy righteousness." Ellicott notes that Paul's quotation "has naturally opened up an avenue for discussion on... free-will and predestination", but holds the immediate purpose simpler — "to contrast the faithfulness of the God of the covenant with the falsehood of the covenant people".

On verse 5 the reading is nearly unanimous. Delitzsch states it plainly: "David here confesses his hereditary sin as the root of his actual sin", moving "backwards from his birth to conception". Clarke names his opponents: a genuine penitent "deplores, not only the transgression, but the carnal mind which is enmity against God", and "notwithstanding all that Grotius and others have said to the contrary, I believe David to speak here of what is commonly called original sin". Gill guards the doctrine at both ends — no personal iniquity of David's parents, no sinfulness infused by the Maker, "seeing God cannot be the author of sin" — and locates it in natural generation: "as soon as ever the mass of human nature was shaped and quickened... sin was in him, and he was in sin". Wesley makes it a figure: "this filthy stream leads me to a corrupt fountain."

Ellicott alone reports the alternatives. The later rabbis, combining it with "the mystery hanging over the origin and name of David's mother", made him born in adultery. But the verse itself "is only a statement of the truth of experience so constantly affirmed in Scripture of hereditary corruption". He concedes the argument for a personal author "seems strong" here, then offers his corporate reading again: the community "may here speak of its far-back idolatrous ancestry as the mother who conceived it in sin".

Verse 6 is the counterweight. Gill takes the truth desired as internal holiness, "in opposition to the corruption of nature before acknowledged"; Wesley makes it an aggravation both ways: original corruption is "contrary to the holy nature and will of God", the actual sin committed "against that knowledge, which God had wrote in his heart". Clarke hears self-accusation: "I am the very reverse of what I should be." Ellicott concludes that "the sincerity and true self-discernment which God requires can only come of spiritual insight, or... divine instruction."
7:
Hyssop sends everyone to the same three rituals, and to different conclusions. Gill lists them — the blood on the doorposts in Egypt, the cleansing of the leper, the purification of one defiled by a corpse — and reads the petition as self-portrait: David "saw himself a guilty creature, and in danger of the destroying angel, and a filthy creature like the leper". Ellicott makes the same connection and subordinates it: hyssop links the verse to the priestly ordinances, "but generally it is a repetition of the former prayer to have the breach made in the covenant-relationship healed."

Clarke renders the verb "thou shalt make a sin-offering for me", describes the leper's rite in full — two clean birds, cedar-wood, scarlet and hyssop, the living bird dipped in the blood of the killed one — and then makes the observation nobody else does: "this ceremony was not performed till the plague of the leprosy had been healed in the leper", its purpose being "to declare to the people that the man was healed". The rite pronounces a cure rather than working one. Henry reads the petition the same way without the ritual argument: "pardon my sins, and let me know that they are pardoned, that I may be restored to those privileges which by sin I have forfeited and lost" — adding the note that governs his reading, that these petitions, "if we do but add, 'for Christ's sake,' are as evangelical as any other". Wesley makes the typology explicit: as lepers are purified by hyssop, "so do thou cleanse me a leprous and polluted creature, by thy grace, and by that blood of Christ, which is signified by those ceremonial usages."

The joy asked in verse 8 is defined by what sin had and had not destroyed. Gill draws the distinction carefully: the love and favour of God "cannot be lost, yet his sensible presence, which puts joy and gladness into the heart, may"; justification is invariable, "yet the comfortable perception of it may be taken away". Clarke asks the same in a sentence — "let me have a full testimony of my reconciliation to thee; that the soul, so deeply distressed by a sense of thy displeasure, may be healed by a sense of thy pardoning mercy" — and Wesley locates the instrument: God should "by thy spirit, seal the pardon of my sins on my conscience".

On the broken bones Ellicott is briefest and best: "through his whole being the psalmist has felt the crushing weight of sin; to its very fibres, as we say, his frame has suffered."

Delitzsch marks the structural turn: "the prayer for justification is followed by the prayer for renewing". A clean heart is one "not beclouded by sin and a consciousness of sin", the word including the conscience; a stedfast spirit is "a spirit certain respecting his state of favour and well-grounded in it". He adds that David's prayer "has reference to the very same thing that is promised by the prophets as a future work of salvation".

The hiding of the face is read as a reversal of the ordinary idiom. Ellicott points it out: this is "thy angry look", where "more usually the expression is used in the opposite sense of hiding the gracious look"; and it matters, since "as long as Jehovah kept the offences before Him the breach in the covenant must continue." Clarke ties it back to the confession: David's sin "was ever before his own face; and he knew that the eye of God was constantly upon him", so "with a just horror of his transgressions" he asks God to turn away and blot them out "so that they may never more be seen". Gill hears a deprecation of chastisement as well as a plea for pardon, the sins being "such that he knew would not bear the examination of justice".
10:
Clarke presses the verb create: "mending will not avail; my heart is altogether corrupted; it must be new made, made as it was in the beginning" — "exactly the sentiment of St. Paul", since what avails is "a new creation". Gill reasons from incapacity: knowing "he could not make his heart clean himself", David entreats a work "which required creating power".

What kind of spirit is asked divides them twice. On right, Ellicott judges "the constant of the margin is nearer the Hebrew, and better"; Wesley renders "firm or constant, that my resolution may be fixed and unmoveable". On free the disagreement is sharper. Clarke reads nobility — "a free, generous, princely spirit; cheerfully giving up itself to thee; no longer bound and degraded by the sinfulness of sin" — and Wesley the same, against a "base and illiberal and disingenuous and servile spirit". Delitzsch reports that "the old expositors thought of" a prince and high rank, with the Greek and Latin behind them, but rules against it: the word "has, however, without any doubt, its ethical sense in this passage". Ellicott agrees, and offers an alternative: "rather, with a willing spirit. Or we may render, a willing spirit shall support me."

"Take not thy holy spirit from me" is where Ellicott records the controversy rather than joining it. Commentators have argued whether it means "the spirit of office given to the king on his anointing" or the spirit of grace, "and Calvinists and Lutherans have made the text a battle-ground of controversy"; but "plainly, as the parallelism shows, the petition is equivalent to a prayer against rejection". He notes the casting-away phrase is elsewhere "used of the formal rejection of Israel by the God of the covenant" — further support, he thinks, for reading the psalm of the community. Clarke makes it the hinge of hope: "while the Spirit stays, painfully convincing of sin, righteousness, and judgment, there is hope of salvation; when it departs, then the hope of redemption is gone."

On the restored joy Clarke makes the observation the others miss: "this is an awful prayer. And why? Because it shows he once had the joy of God's salvation; and had lost it by sin!" Ellicott reads covenant privilege restored; Gill distinguishes the salvation itself, which "can never fail", from the joy of it.

Spurgeon turns the vow to teach into a doctrine of ministry: none "instruct others so well as those who have been experimentally taught of God themselves. Reclaimed poachers make the best gamekeepers." The degree of "Sinner Saved" is "more needful for a soul-winning evangelist" than any academic one, his "matter" being taught "in the school of experience". Clarke borrows an exclamation: "who can confide in his own strength, when he sees David fall? Who can despair of Divine mercy when he sees him forgiven?"

Bloodguiltiness is read four ways. Henry names the crime without softening it — David had "slain Uriah with the sword of the children of Ammon" — and observes that he "perhaps had stopped the mouth of conscience with that frivolous excuse, that he did not kill him himself; but now he was convinced that he was the murderer". Clarke agrees this is the phrase that "gives most color to the propriety of the title". Delitzsch insists on the plain word: David "does not seek to lessen his guilt; he calls it by its right name", a word "which signifies blood violently shed". Gill takes it of the threatened slaughter in David's family; Ellicott alone proposes emendation, the plural leaving it unclear whether blood shed or violence anticipated is meant: "probably we should read 'from death'". On the opened lips Clarke marks the order — David "could not praise God for pardon till he felt that God had pardoned him" — and Ellicott closes: "the sense of forgiveness is like a glad morning to song-birds."
16:
Why sacrifice is refused is answered from the law itself, not from prophecy. Gill states the fact in a clause: "there was no sacrifice appointed under the law for murder and adultery." Wesley says the same: the words are "not to be understood absolutely, with respect to David's crimes, which were not to be expiated by any sacrifice". Clarke draws out the conditional buried in the verse — "nor hast thou appointed in the law any sacrifices to atone for deliberate murder and adultery: if thou hadst, I would cheerfully have given them to thee" — and closes: "the matter is before thee as Judge."

Ellicott reads the verse corporately, as he has the whole psalm. The rabbinical commentators make David's penitence take "the place of the sin-offering prescribed by the Law", but "in the mouth of an individual, language with such an intention would not have been possible". To an exiled nation "deprived of the legal rites, and by that very deprivation compelled to look beyond their outward form to their inner spirit, the words are most appropriate."

The broken spirit is expounded by Clarke through the Hebrew and by Henry through the doctrine. Clarke notes the first verb "signifies exactly the same as our word shiver, to break into pieces, to reduce into splinters", and sets the whole in a disjunction: the crimes admitting no legal atonement, they are reserved "to be punished by exemplary acts of justice, or to be pardoned by a sovereign act of mercy". Henry states the impossibility that makes the sacrifice necessary — the penitent "cannot make satisfaction for sin", so "God cannot take any satisfaction in them" — and enters the qualification the psalm does not supply: "the broken heart is acceptable to God only through Jesus Christ; there is no true repentance without faith in him." Gill takes the breaking evangelically, the penitent "grieving for sin as committed against a God of love... while beholding a pierced and wounded Saviour". Wesley reduces it to a comparison: "this is of more value than many sacrifices."

The last two verses raise the psalm's second question of authorship, and the answers run the range. Clarke is most decided: they "most evidently refer to the time of the captivity, when the walls of Jerusalem were broken down, and the temple service entirely discontinued; and, consequently, are long posterior to the times of David" — whence "it has been concluded that the Psalm was not composed by David... and that the title must be that of some other Psalm inadvertently affixed to this." Ellicott records the same difficulty and its ancient pedigree — an early father "long ago saying that they better suited the exiles in Babylon", so the verses "have been regarded as a liturgical addition, such as doubtless the compiler made". Then he turns the argument round: it is "not only these two verses which harmonise with the feelings of the restored exiles, but the whole psalm".

Gill reports two Jewish alternatives without adopting either — that a Spanish rabbi thought the verses added during the captivity, and that others took them as David's prophecy of "the acceptableness of sacrifices in the times of the Messiah". Wesley takes the prayer at face value and hears one more note of penitence: build the walls and let the temple be built "notwithstanding my sins".

On the sacrifices that will then please, Gill insists they "must be different from the legal ones he desired not", the word then tying the verse back to the refusal: the sacrifice of Christ first, then the saints presenting "their bodies to him a holy, living, and acceptable sacrifice". Delitzsch gives the structural reason for the return: from the spiritual sacrifice the psalm "comes back to the material sacrifices that are offered in a right state of mind", David's prayer for himself here passing over into prayer for the city.
